overview: Hong Taiji proclaimed the Qing dynastic name in 1636, and Qing rulers established their court in Beijing in 1644. Their empire brought many peoples under a Manchu ruling house. The dynasty ended with abdication in 1912. The imported 1650 to 1920 range therefore extends beyond imperial rule. Its early Taiwan features also group the separately labelled Middag Kingdom under Qing; these coarse shapes must not be treated as evidence of continuous Qing control.

periods.title: Before the Beijing court
periods.summary: The Qing dynastic name was adopted before the conquest of Beijing.

periods.title: The Qing imperial era from Beijing
periods.summary: Expansion, internal changes and upheavals culminated in the end of imperial government.

sections.title: A vast empire and its public image

items.text: Qianlong’s empire extended across Tibet and large areas of Central Asia. He presented himself differently to different subjects: as a learned patron to Han Chinese scholars, as a steppe prince to Mongols, and as a Buddhist sacred figure to Tibetans. These were deliberate claims to authority over varied communities, rather than evidence that everyone welcomed Qing rule.

The artist Wang Hui supervised great painted scrolls commemorating Kangxi’s southern inspection tour of 1689. They included the emperor’s arrival at Mount Tai and entry into Suzhou. Roads, boats, cities and crowds fill these court-sponsored images. They are valuable pictures of a landscape and a powerful ruler’s preferred public image, rather than a neutral opinion poll about his popularity.

sections.title: Feeding households and earning a living

items.text: Qing officials used grain reserves and trade to respond to harvest failures. River transport could bring food into some regions relatively easily; inland districts were harder and more expensive to supply. Emergency granaries were especially important where markets and transport could not quickly fill the gap. Storing money was useful, but a hungry family still needed actual grain.

In some prosperous, densely settled districts, women devoted more work to spinning and weaving cloth for sale. Households could buy goods they previously made themselves, using money from textile production. Officials promoted cotton-growing and weaving instruction; illustrated materials showed stages such as picking cotton and working a loom. Domestic work could connect a family closely to distant markets.

Yin Yu Tang, built around 1800 for a merchant family in Huizhou, had sixteen bedrooms around shared spaces and a central courtyard. Carved lattice windows overlooked fish ponds. The house survives today at the Peabody Essex Museum after being moved from China. Its long occupation continued beyond the Qing, so furnishings and alterations belong to several generations of family history.

In Huizhou’s merchant families, boys might leave in their early teens to apprentice with relatives or family contacts in another city. Women, younger children and elders kept the household going while merchants spent long periods away. Family reunions at the Mid-Autumn Festival could therefore carry special meaning. Commercial success had a very personal cost in time spent apart.

A silk fragment dated around 1875 is covered with tiny writing in black and red ink. Powerhouse Museum identifies it as a concealed aid for an imperial examination candidate: passages from the Chinese classics worn as garment lining. Its width is only 16.5 centimetres. Preparing for exams took learning and practice; this object records someone’s plan for an unauthorized shortcut.

A manuscript from around 1805 describes smallpox vaccination as practised at Guangzhou, then often called Canton. Surgeon Alexander Pearson prepared the account, George Thomas Staunton translated it for Chinese readers, and a local merchant helped publish it. The Royal Society preserves the English manuscript. Sharing a medical technique depended on translators, publishers and local networks as well as doctors.

A nineteenth-century shuttlecock from Shanghai, now in the British Museum, was made from cotton and feathers. Players kicked it with their feet to keep it airborne. The surviving toy gives a wonderfully simple glimpse of recreation: feet did the work usually given to a racket. The museum dates this example broadly to the 1800s.

A porcelain ritual vessel in the Royal Collection carries “大清乾隆年製”, meaning “Made in the Qianlong reign of the Great Qing”. This is Chinese written on its base in seal script, transcribed here in ordinary modern type. The eighteenth-century vessel, RCIN 58813.1, was made at Jingdezhen. Its mark connects a workshop’s product with an imperial reign.

A vase dated 1744 in the National Palace Museum contains another vase inside it. Turning the neck rotates the inner vessel, allowing its blue lotus decoration to move behind openings in the outer shell. Yellow enamels and gold details decorate the outside. Firing and fitting the separate porcelain parts demanded precision: this is a moving artwork powered by a hand, not a hidden motor.

The later Qing period brought devastating rebellions and foreign wars, alongside striking changes in everyday communication. Photography and lithographic printing expanded the ways people could make and encounter images. Telegraphs, railways and electricity also entered a society still containing many older forms of work and transport. These changes were uneven, rather than a simultaneous transformation of every town and village.

ending.text: The Wuchang uprising of October 1911 was followed by provinces withdrawing their allegiance to the Qing government. On 12 February 1912, the emperor abdicated, ending the dynasty’s imperial rule as a republic replaced it. Communities, families and many cultural practices continued amid further political upheaval. The map’s 1920 endpoint is a coverage error, not an additional eight years of Qing government.
